blueprint_topic: Management of Care — clinical-trial participant safety, protocol adherence, documentation, and research-team coordination
stem: A client enrolled in an oncology investigational-drug trial calls the research nurse between scheduled visits to report a new severe symptom. Which action best reflects the oncology clinical research nurse's role?

options.A: Assess the symptom and clinical urgency, document the event, contact the investigator/study team per protocol, and coordinate needed care and safety reporting.
options.B: Document the symptom for routine study review when it is a listed expected toxicity, while directing the client to the usual oncology team for symptom management.
options.C: Complete symptom assessment and arrange clinical care first, then update the research team at the next scheduled visit if the symptom improves before then.
options.D: Enter the symptom in the research record and wait for the investigator to assess its significance before the nurse performs further clinical assessment or coordination.

rationale: A is correct. ONS describes oncology clinical research nursing as requiring precise protocol adherence, adverse-event monitoring and reporting, detailed documentation, clinical judgment, and coordination of care. FDA's December 2025 final investigator-safety-reporting guidance states that investigators must immediately report serious adverse events to the sponsor under 21 CFR 312.64(b), while nonserious adverse events are recorded and reported according to the protocol timetable. A report of a new severe symptom should therefore trigger clinical assessment, documentation, and prompt use of the study's protocol-defined safety/escalation pathway rather than an assumption that severity alone establishes the regulatory category. B is incorrect because an event being expected or listed does not justify deferring assessment or protocol-directed reporting of a newly severe symptom to routine review. C is incorrect because clinical care and research-safety communication are coordinated responsibilities; the research team should not be left uninformed until a future visit solely because symptoms may improve. D is incorrect because CRN practice includes clinical assessment, adverse-event monitoring, and care coordination rather than documentation alone while waiting for the investigator to perform all clinical evaluation.
educational_objective: When a clinical-trial participant reports a new severe symptom, assess clinical urgency, document accurately, use the protocol-defined adverse-event/safety pathway, communicate with the investigator/research team, and coordinate needed care without assuming that symptom severity alone determines regulatory seriousness.
source_organization: Oncology Nursing Society (ONS); U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
source_document_title: Ready to Manage Clinical Trials? Here's How to Grow Your Competence From Novice to Expert; Investigator Responsibilities — Safety Reporting for Investigational Drugs and Devices
source_version_date: ONS article published January 15, 2026; FDA final guidance issued December 2025 and confirmed in FDA FY2026 reporting; sources rechecked 2026-08-20
source_locator: ONS January 15, 2026 article, body paragraphs under the clinical-research-nurse competency discussion: oncology trials require precise protocol adherence, complex adverse-event monitoring/reporting, detailed and rigorous documentation, and coordination of care; early CRN task mastery includes documentation/care coordination, and competency domains include patient safety, trial coordination, regulatory knowledge, data integrity, and communication. FDA December 2025 final guidance — Introduction, PDF page 3: guidance helps investigators comply with 21 CFR 312.64(b) and 312.66 and identifies SAEs requiring immediate sponsor reporting. Sections V.A-V.D, especially PDF pages 8-10: investigator must immediately report any SAE to sponsor under §312.64(b); 'immediately' is interpreted as as soon as feasible after recognizing an SAE and obtaining relevant information; nonserious adverse events are recorded and reported to the sponsor according to the protocol timetable. FDA also distinguishes adverse-event severity/clinical description from the regulatory serious-adverse-event criteria in the guidance definitions.
source_claim_supported: Current ONS guidance supports protocol adherence, adverse-event monitoring/reporting, rigorous documentation, clinical judgment, and care coordination as core oncology CRN functions. Current FDA guidance requires investigator safety reporting under §312.64(b) and protocol-based reporting of nonserious events, supporting prompt assessment/escalation without treating the adjective 'severe' as automatically equivalent to a regulatory SAE.
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care — Collaboration with Multidisciplinary Team, Client Rights/Safety, Continuity of Care, Concepts of Management, and legal/organizational standards: assess and communicate significant findings, coordinate care with appropriate team members, follow organizational/protocol requirements, document care accurately, and protect client safety within nursing scope.
pdf_visual_verification: FDA December 2025 final guidance PDF page 9/file page 10 was visually verified by screenshot on 2026-08-20 and visibly showed the Timing of Serious Adverse Event Reporting section: investigator must immediately report any SAE to the sponsor, with 'immediately' interpreted as as soon as feasible and initial reporting timing recommended in the protocol. The ONS evidence is current HTML and requires no PDF screenshot. Relevant NCSBN 2026 Management of Care content had been visually verified earlier in this audit session.
targeted_near_duplicate_check: Repository-targeted search for 'oncology investigational drug adverse event research nurse protocol investigator severe symptom documentation reporting' returned no indexed matching files; no near-duplicate identified by the targeted check.
correction_summary: Retained the participant-reported symptom construct but removed the uniquely long key and cartoon errors involving independent dose changes, waiting until a routine visit, or omitting known adverse effects. The revised distractors test realistic failures to integrate research and clinical responsibilities: deferring an expected event to routine review, postponing research-team communication until after symptom care, and reducing the CRN role to documentation while awaiting investigator assessment. The rebuild also avoids equating clinical severity with the regulatory SAE definition.

option_audit.A: Correct; integrates ONS-supported clinical assessment/documentation/care coordination with protocol-defined research safety communication and FDA investigator-reporting requirements.
option_audit.B: Plausible expected-toxicity error; incorrect because expectedness does not make a newly severe symptom suitable for routine review without prompt assessment and protocol-directed safety handling.
option_audit.C: Plausible clinical-care-first sequencing error; incorrect because clinical care and research safety communication should be coordinated rather than separating study-team notification until a later scheduled visit.
option_audit.D: Plausible investigator-authority misconception; incorrect because investigator oversight does not reduce the CRN role to data entry; CRN practice includes assessment, adverse-event monitoring and care coordination.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on always/never/only/all/must-type distractor absolutes.
cueing_audit.answer_length: All four alternatives contain comparable clinical-trial safety and coordination detail; the key is not uniquely signaled by length.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four alternatives are parallel responses to the same between-visit participant safety report.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: No defensible second answer identified after current ONS/FDA source-based audit and targeted repository search.
